Senses.Explanation: The Caodong Five Ranks are a named five-part scheme associated with Dongshan Liangjie and Caoshan Benji. Miyun Yuanwu contrasts them with Linji Yixuan's Three Mysteries. Unnamed monks ask Caoshan Benji for the ranks; Huiyan Zhizhao and Foguo explain five-part formulations; Wuhuan Xingchong and Sanyi Mingyu raise them in their own exchanges. A compiler introduces Dongshan's rank verses, and Layman Zhang Dangong questions Liangting Jingting about the scheme. The passages frame the ranks through upright and crooked, ruler and minister, merit, princes, or facing the guest. The headword names the fivefold scheme, while the particular paired terms specify its formulation.

Senses.Explanation: The five ranks of lord and minister are the named Caodong set arranging five paired positions through lord-and-minister language. Gulin Qingmao places the set beside the three mysteries, and Huishan Jiexian discusses it as a named framework. Ruibai Mingxue uses it in an incense formula, Liangting Jingting debates later ordering of the ranks, and Hanyue Fazang sets out his own correspondence. The entry records the set without imposing a solution on it.

Senses.Explanation: The five Chan houses are an institutional grouping of lineages and their recorded modes of address: Guiyang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan. Zhongfeng Mingben states the controlling distinction directly: “what are called the five houses are five in their people, not five in their Way” (所云五家者，乃五家其人，非五家其道也); he also traces them from the two streams of Nanyue and Qingyuan to five people. The label appears in compounds for five-house lineages and five-house purports, and expands to “five houses and seven lineages” (五家七宗). Yuanwu Keqin criticizes people for dividing this into five houses and seven lineages and erecting separate gateways, while the Yongzheng Emperor answers a question about “one purport, five lineages” by saying they are the same when correct and different when deviant.
